---
title: "Tutorial: Customizing *ggplot* figures"
number-sections: true
---

## About

This tutorial shows how to use additional commands in *ggplot2* to customize figures.

I recommend that you create your own RStudio project with a new Quarto document to work through this tutorial.

## Setup

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## Acquire data

Let's make some continuous data that have different degrees of relatedness.

```{r}
#| label: x-y-error
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| 
n_pts = 600
x <- rnorm(n = n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1)
y_25 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.25)
y_50 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.50)
y_75 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.75)
y_100 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1)
y_125 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1.25)
y_150 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1.50)

df <- data.frame(x = rep(x, 6), 
                 y = c(y_25, y_50, y_75, y_100, y_125, y_150), 
                 noise = c(.25, .50, .75, 1.00, 1.25, 1.50), 
                 each = n_pts)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Change any variable you like

One powerful way to learn a new skill is to take sample code, alter it, and see what happens.
Here, you could change the `n_pts` variable to see how the figures look with different number of points.
:::

## Visualize

### Basic scatterplot

In @fig-0.0, I filter the bigger dataset using the `filter(noise == 0.25)` command.
This selects the subset where the noise is 0.25.

::: {.callout-note}
## Troubleshooting

Make sure that your Quarto document's `Setup` chunk has `library(dplyr)` in it.
Alternatively, you could change the `filter(noise == 0.25)` line to `dplyr::filter(noise == 0.25)`.
This tells R to find and use *dplyr* even if you haven't run `library(dplyr)` in your Quarto document.

If this fails, then you may need to install *dplyr*.
In your R console, outside of your Quarto document, run `install.packages("dplyr")`.
Then go back and render your Quarto document.

Think of the problem this way.
Let's say that your friend says "I have to call Mike."
But you know lots of Mike's, so unless it's obvious from context which Mike you're talking about, things could go sideways.
By telling R `library(dplyr)`, we're saying that we're talking about `filter()` from the *dplyr* package, not some other `filter()` command.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.0
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point()
```

### Adjust alpha

In @fig-0.1 I try reducing clutter by adjusting alpha.
The `alpha` parameter controls the saturation (intensity) of the dots based on how many points overlap.
Lower values of alpha mean that more points have to overlap for that point to appear darker or more saturated.
Notice that the alpha parameter belongs with `geom_point()`.
If we had other layers, say lines or annotations, these could have their own alpha levels.

Here I tried `alpha = 0.3`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.1
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3)
```

## Change theme

In @fig-0.2 I eliminate the gray background, by adding a theme.
There are many *ggplot2* themes, but `theme_classic()` is a decent place to start.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.2
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Add labels

In @fig-0.3, I keep the previous changes and add some labels using `labs()`, short for labels.
Notice that the `labs()` function has a parameter for `title`, `subtitle`, and `caption`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.3
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.")
```

### Change text size

The text is small.
In @fig-0.3.1, I adjust it with another `theme()` command.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.3.1
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

Read the help document about the `labs()` command to learn more.
Enter `help("labs")` into your R console.

## Add best-fitting line

In @fig-0.4 we add a best-fitting line using `geom_smooth(method = "lm")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.4
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.",
       subtitle = "y = x + N(0, .25).",
       caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

## Add annotation

In @fig-0.5 we add an annotations featuring the the correlation (`r` value) using `annotate()`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.5
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

xy_corr <- with(df, cor.test(x, y))

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.",
       subtitle = "y = x + N(0, .25).",
       caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text",
           x = -2,
           y = 3,
           label = "r = .89") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

### Grab correlation

Add an annotation with the correlation using `annotate()`, but grab the correlation from a variable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.5.1
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

xy_corr <- with(df, cor.test(x, y))

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.",
       subtitle = "y = x + N(0, .25).",
       caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = -1,
    y = 3,
    label = paste0("r = ", xy_corr$estimate)
  ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What the coordinates mean in `annotate()`

You might notice that the x and y coordinates we give to the `annotate()` layer specify the *middle* point of the text for our annotation.
:::

### Format annotation

The correlation value has too many digits, so let's fix that.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.5.2
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

xy_corr <- with(df, cor.test(x,y))
corr_r <- xy_corr$estimate |>
  format(digits = 3)

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 3, label = paste0("r = ", corr_r)) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

### Extend annotation

Add a *p* value and degrees of freedom to the annotation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.5.3
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df_25 <- filter(df, noise == .25)

xy_corr <- with(df_25, cor.test(x,y))
corr_r <- xy_corr$estimate |>
  format(digits = 3)
sample_n <- xy_corr$parameter
p_value <- format(xy_corr$p.value, digits = 3)
est_lo <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[1], digits = 2)
est_hi <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[2], digits = 2)

corr_text <- paste0("r(", sample_n, ")=", corr_r, ", p=", p_value)

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 3.75, label = corr_text) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

### Different noise level

Let's try one with a different noise level.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.5.4
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df_150 <- filter(df, noise == 1.50)

xy_corr <- with(df_150, cor.test(x,y))
corr_r <- xy_corr$estimate |>
  format(digits = 3)
sample_n <- xy_corr$parameter
p_value <- format(xy_corr$p.value, digits = 3)
est_lo <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[1], digits = 2)
est_hi <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[2], digits = 2)

corr_text <- paste0("r(", sample_n, ")=", corr_r, ", p=", p_value)

df_150 |>
  # filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, 1.50).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 3.75, label = corr_text) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

## Facets

Let's take the gist of @fig-0.5.2 and make a plot with multiple facets based on the amount of random noise added to `y`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-0.6
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

df_categorical_noise <- df |>
  mutate(noise_cat = ordered(noise))

df_categorical_noise |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(facets = ~ noise_cat, ncol = 3) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line at various levels of random noise.") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))
```

## Assigning names

In the next series of figures, we'll take advantage of a cool feature of the *ggplot2* syntax: Assigning figures to a variable.
This can make the process of exploring different figure options much easier.

So, in @fig-1.0 below we give a very basic plot a name: `p`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.0
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false

p <- df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point()

p
```

Now, we can "add" new layers or themese to the base figure using the syntax indicated below.

### Add a layer

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.1
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
p + theme_classic()

p_classic <- p + theme_classic()
```

### Add a line

@fig-1.2 adds a smooth, best-fitting line to @fig-1.1.
Note that in the previous code gave @fig-1.1 the name `p_classic`.
This let's us "add" the `geom_smooth()` to `p_classic` as indicated below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.2
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
p_classic + geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

### Dark theme

We can use this syntax to explore the space of features we want for our plot.
@fig-1.3 tries `theme_dark()`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.3
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
p + theme_dark() + geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

### Light theme

@fig-1.4 tries `theme_light()`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.4
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
p + theme_light() + geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```
